926fd9d3.title: 1. The 60-second test that shocks practices
926fd9d3.html:
⏱ 5 minutes · 🎯 Your AI search score out of 3, plus a written list of the practices AI is currently recommending instead of you.

More and more patients don't Google "dentist near me" any more. They ask ChatGPT, Google's AI or Siri: "Who's the best dentist in my town?" The AI gives them two or three names, and that's who they call.

Hardly anyone in dentistry is talking about this yet. That's your head start.

🧪 Do this right now (60 seconds):

1. Open ChatGPT in a new chat.

2. Type: "Who's the best dentist in [your town]?"

3. Then: "[Your main treatment, e.g. Invisalign] in [your town]"

4. Then: "Emergency dentist in [your town]"

Are you mentioned? Who is? Write the names down. That's the competition AI is sending your patients to.

✅ Action step

Post your result in the discussion: "Mentioned in X out of 3." No judgement. Most practices score 0 the first time, and that's exactly what this course fixes.

❓ Questions or a win to share? Join the discussion:

3. Post your result in the discussion as "Mentioned in X out of 3."

926fd9d3.title: 2. Get your AI visibility score
926fd9d3.html:
⏱ 10 minutes · 🎯 Your practice website's AI visibility score, which band it sits in, and your 5 weakest sections written down ready to fix.

Now let's see why. Every website can be scored on how easily AI can read and quote it. Our scoring checks things like whether your pages give clear answers, name your town and treatments, include real facts, and make sense to a machine as well as a person.

📊 What the scores mean:

• Under 35: AI can barely read you. Usually the site is mostly images, sliders or "welcome to our website" text.

• 35–60: AI can read you, but you're easy to skip.

• 60–75: strong. This is where the practices AI recommends tend to sit.

Nobody honest promises 100, and nobody can promise first place on ChatGPT.

926fd9d3.title: 3. 5 fixes that beat the practice down the road
926fd9d3.html:
⏱ 15 minutes · 🎯 A completed check of your website and Google Business Profile against the five fixes, with one fix chosen and started this week.

Most dental websites lose on the same five things. Fix these and you're ahead of most practices in your area.

1️⃣ Words, not pictures. If your opening hours, prices or treatments only appear in an image or a slider, AI can't read them. Put them in plain text.

2️⃣ Say where you are and what you do. "Riverside Dental is an NHS and private practice in Bristol offering implants, Invisalign and emergency appointments" beats "Welcome to our friendly practice".

3️⃣ Real facts. Years open, number of dentists, prices from £, how fast new patients are seen. Facts get quoted; fluff gets skipped.

4️⃣ An FAQ section. Answer what patients actually ask: cost, NHS availability, emergencies, nervous patients, parking, finance.

5️⃣ Your Google Business Profile, complete and consistent. The same name, address and phone everywhere, the right category, photos, every treatment listed, and replies to reviews.

✅ Action step

Pick one fix and do it this week. Post "done ✅" with which one.

❓ Questions or a win to share? Join the discussion:

3. Choose one of the five fixes, put it in your diary for this week, and post "done ✅" in the community when it's finished.

858a9618.title: 1. Grow from the patients you already have
858a9618.html:
⏱ 15 minutes · 🎯 A clear picture of which marketing consent you hold, plus a plan to reach three groups already on your list: patients with missing teeth or dentures, patients suited to a service plan, and patients with birthdays coming up.

The easiest growth is usually sitting in your own patient list. These ideas come from years of running real practices.

🦷 Patients with missing teeth or dentures: pull a list of patients who've had extractions, have gaps or wear dentures. They're the people most likely to want to hear about implants.

📅 Service plans: offer a plan to every suitable patient after their treatment, so they come back regularly and spread the cost.

🎂 Birthday offers: send patients a birthday offer (for example money off a treatment).

⚖️ Do it properly: only send marketing to patients who've agreed to hear from you, keep it honest, and follow the GDC and advertising rules for dental marketing. If you're unsure whether your consent records cover it, check before you send.

✅ Action steps

2. Check what marketing consent you hold and how it's recorded.

858a9618.title: 2. Reviews that bring in new patients
858a9618.html:
⏱ 10 minutes · 🎯 Your Google review link copied and ready, an automatic post-appointment text drafted, and today's review count noted so you can track progress over 30 days.

New patients read reviews before they book, and Google and AI assistants use them to decide who to recommend.

📲 Ask every time: send an automatic text after each appointment with a direct link to your Google review page. Most happy patients will leave a review if you make it one tap.

🏆 Get the team involved: run a friendly staff competition for asking patients for reviews.

⚠️ One rule: never offer patients anything in return for a review. Google doesn't allow it, and it can get reviews removed. Reward your team for asking, not patients for posting.

💬 Reply to every review, good and bad, politely and without patient details.

✅ Action steps

ffc6e574.title: 1. What AI can take off your plate
ffc6e574.html:
⏱ 10 minutes · 🎯 A short list of the 3 jobs you most often forget or put off, each sorted into checking, reminding, drafting or chasing, so you can see where AI could help first.

AI isn't about replacing your team. It's about taking the repetitive, easy-to-forget jobs off the people who are already stretched. Here's what we use at Teething Issues every day.

📋 Compliance checking: Bobby, our AI compliance system, reads real practice documents and spots what's missing, expired or likely to be flagged at inspection, across areas like staff files, audits and risk assessments.

📞 An assistant for calls, emails and diaries: Jarvis handles messages and admin, and flags only what needs a human.

📣 Outreach that runs itself: our own outreach checks dental websites and sends a small number of carefully checked emails every weekday, with no one pressing send.

ffc6e574.title: 2. Using AI safely in a dental practice
ffc6e574.html:
⏱ 15 minutes · 🎯 A short written AI policy for your team, plus a clear picture of which AI tools are already being used in your practice.

AI is powerful, but a dental practice holds sensitive information, so a few ground rules matter.

🔒 Keep patient-identifiable information out of free, public AI tools. Don't paste in names, dates of birth or clinical notes.

🏢 Use business accounts, and check what each tool does with your data and where it's stored.

🧾 Under UK GDPR you're responsible for how patient and staff data is used. For anything involving personal data, think about whether a data protection impact assessment is needed.

👀 Check everything AI writes before it goes to a patient or into a record. It can sound confident and still be wrong.

📄 Give your team a short AI policy: what tools are allowed, what data never goes in, and who to ask.

The Bobby tools in the Circle run on your own computer, in your own account, so your documents aren't sent to us.

9cd896ec.title: 1. The staff file every role needs
9cd896ec.html:
⏱ 15 minutes · 🎯 Your whole team sorted into the four role groups, with one staff file checked against the right list and its gaps marked.

CQC checks staff files under Regulation 19 (fit and proper persons). The trick is knowing exactly what each role needs, no more and no less.

👥 Four role groups (each one needs everything the group before it needs, plus a bit more):

• Non-clinical: receptionist, practice manager, treatment coordinator, cleaner.

• Unqualified clinical: trainee dental nurse.

• Qualified clinical: GDC-registered dental nurse.

• Clinician: dentist (including specialists), hygienist, therapist.

📁 Everyone needs: photo ID, right to work, proof of address, staff details form, medical history form, Enhanced DBS, CV, two references, job offer letter (best practice), signed contract, job description, induction checklist and an annual appraisal.

➕ Clinical staff also need: Hep B evidence and a personal development plan.

➕ Registered staff also need: GDC certificate, indemnity and qualification certificates.

➕ Clinicians at NHS practices also need: a performer letter.

🗓️ The pre-2014 rule: staff who started at your practice before 2014 don't need a contract, CV, references or qualification certificates on file. It follows the person's start date, so it survives a change of owner.

🛑 Hard stop: anyone who should be GDC-registered but isn't cannot work (trainee nurses aside).

✅ Action steps

1. List your team and put each person in one of the four groups.

2. Pick one staff file and check it against the list above.

3. Post in the discussion: which document is most often missing in your files?

9cd896ec.title: 2. 5 staff-file mistakes inspectors find
9cd896ec.html:
⏱ 15 minutes · 🎯 Every staff file checked against the 5 common inspection mistakes (plus GDC expiry), with each gap marked and a fix noted.

These are the mistakes Bobby finds again and again in real staff files. Check yours for each one.

1️⃣ A Hep B vaccination card with no blood test. The card alone isn't enough. Clinical staff need a blood test showing an antibody level (titre) of 100 mIU/mL or more before any exposure-prone work.

2️⃣ The wrong DBS. It must be an Enhanced DBS, with the disclosure fields reading "none recorded". CQC likes it renewed every 3 years (a preference, not the law), or you can use the DBS Update Service. If it's missing or pending, complete an "Awaiting DBS" risk assessment.

3️⃣ Weak references. You need two, covering the last 3 years: one from the current or most recent employer. Friends and family never count. If one employer covers the whole 3 years, the second reference must come from a different person there.

4️⃣ A contract that isn't really finished. Look for another practice's name left in the template, [placeholders] never filled in, a missing employer signature, and no conditions-of-employment clause (Hep B, GDC, indemnity, DBS, CPD). Many standard templates leave that clause out.

5️⃣ An induction signed by one side. Both the person who ran it and the new starter should sign, section by section, not with one tick at the end.

Bonus: an out-of-date GDC certificate. Read the expiry from the sentence after the person's name, not the first date on the page.

✅ Action steps

2. Open one contract and read it properly, start to finish.

9cd896ec.title: 3. Induction, appraisals and the Wisdom Trail
9cd896ec.html:
⏱ 15 minutes · 🎯 A list of every team member's last appraisal date, with overdue ones booked and a simple Wisdom Trail check showing how each appraisal links to a PDP and CPD.

A file full of documents isn't the goal. CQC wants to see that you develop your people.

🧭 Induction: cover each area properly (for example GDPR, cross-infection and fire), and have both people sign each section. It protects the new starter and the practice.

📋 Annual appraisal: a look back at the year. A good one has an objective review of performance, reflection from both sides, a check of the person's GDC scope of practice, and signatures and dates.

🎯 Personal development plan (PDP): a look forward. It follows the GDC's enhanced CPD approach: SMART goals, the GDC's recommended topics, training needs and target dates.

🧵 The Wisdom Trail: gaps spotted in the appraisal become goals in the PDP, which match the CPD certificates added later in the year. Appraisal → PDP → CPD. It won't always line up perfectly, and that's fine, but it's exactly what inspectors love to see.

✅ Action steps

9cd896ec.title: 4. Delegate with named leads
9cd896ec.html:
⏱ 15 minutes · 🎯 A completed one-page "who's responsible for what" sheet naming a lead for every key role, ready to display in your staff room.

Owners and managers burn out when every job lands on them. Named leads share the load, and CQC expects many of them anyway.

🧑‍⚕️ Roles to name in your practice:

• Radiation Protection Supervisor

• Infection control (cross-infection) lead

• First aider

• Health and safety lead

• Safeguarding lead

• CQC Registered Manager and Nominated Individual

• Fire wardens

• Information governance lead / Data Protection Officer

• Person who reports significant events

📌 Put it on one page: a simple "who's responsible for what" sheet, displayed where the team can see it. Inspectors often ask staff "who is your safeguarding lead?" or "who is your RPS?", and everyone should be able to answer.

🤝 Delegate the outcome, not just the task: "you own the weekly emergency kit check, logged every Friday" works far better than "can you check the kit?".

75598002.title: 1. How a CQC dental inspection actually works
75598002.html:
⏱ 20 minutes · 🎯 A first draft of your 10–15 minute opening talk and a named person ready to upload documents to the CQC portal, so you know exactly what happens from the first call to the final report.

Knowing exactly what happens takes most of the fear out of an inspection. Here's the real process, step by step.

📅 Notice: you usually get about 2 weeks' written notice. Unannounced visits are rare, and only happen after serious whistleblowing or an immediate safety concern.

💻 Before the visit: the lead inspector calls your Registered Manager and sends a portal link. Expect to upload key documents within a few days, such as your Statement of Purpose, latest infection control audit and Legionella risk assessment. More and more evidence is now sent before the day, so there's less paperwork on site.

👥 Who comes: a lead CQC inspector plus a Specialist Dental Advisor (a practising dentist or very experienced dental nurse). The lead inspector works through HR files, health and safety and policies. The advisor spends the day in your surgeries and decon room, watching and asking your clinical team directly.

🎤 On the day: you may be asked for a 10–15 minute opening talk covering your history, opening hours, NHS and private mix, team, special treatments, community work, and what you think you do well and want to improve. They'll speak to your manager, receptionists, nurses and dentists.

🗣️ Feedback: verbal feedback is usually given at the end of the day, with written feedback shortly after. You then get a draft report through the CQC Provider Portal with a 17-working-day window to correct factual mistakes. If recommendations are made, an improvement plan is usually due within about 2 weeks of the final report.

⚖️ How you're judged: dental practices don't get a public rating badge. Each area is judged either "Regulations met" or "Not all regulations met". One breach in one area is enough for "not met", so it pays to be solid everywhere rather than brilliant in a few places.

✅ Action steps

1. Write your 10–15 minute opening talk now, using the headings above. It's far easier without an inspection date hanging over you.

2. Check who would upload documents to the portal if the call came tomorrow.

3. Post in the discussion: what's the one part of an inspection that worries you most?

75598002.title: 2. The 10 areas inspectors check
75598002.html:
⏱ 10 minutes · 🎯 A score out of 10 for your practice across the 10 areas CQC inspectors check, with your weakest area identified and one fix booked this week.

Every CQC dental inspection comes back to the same 10 areas. These come from our original Teething Issues CQC Pre-Inspection Checklist and line up with the CQC regulations.

1️⃣ Staff recruitment: right to work, ID, contracts, immunisations, references, Enhanced DBS, GDC and indemnity (Regulation 19).

2️⃣ Staff training: medical emergencies, infection control, safeguarding, IR(ME)R, fire, data protection, learning disability and autism awareness, sepsis.

3️⃣ COSHH: hazardous products identified, safety data sheets, assessments done.

4️⃣ Medical emergency kit: the right drugs and sizes, in date, checked every week.

5️⃣ Servicing: X-ray, fire equipment, boiler, autoclaves, compressors, PAT, fixed wiring.

6️⃣ Audits: infection control, radiographs, record-keeping, disability access, antimicrobial prescribing, each with an action plan.

7️⃣ Risk assessments: fire and Legionella (at least one done externally), health and safety, sharps, plus laser and lone working where they apply.

8️⃣ Practice signage: the full set of notices, flowcharts and posters.

9️⃣ Sedation, if you offer it: trained team, ILS in date.

🔟 CCTV, if you have it: signage, policy and a data protection impact assessment.

The rule that catches most practices: tick an item only when it's present, current and in date. "We've got one somewhere" doesn't count.

75598002.title: 3. Inspection day: set the day up, not just the paperwork
75598002.html:
⏱ 8 minutes · 🎯 A one-page inspection day plan covering diaries, staffing, emergency kit and the morning huddle, ready to use the moment the call comes.

Most practices prepare the folders and forget the day itself. These 8 steps come straight from years of running real inspections, and they take the stress out of it.

1. Keep the diaries light. Book fewer patients, so your team isn't juggling production pressure and inspectors at the same time.

2. Run with fewer dentists. Less clinical activity means fewer people pulled between patients and inspectors.

3. Have senior staff in. Someone confident should always be free to walk with the inspectors and find evidence.

4. No difficult patients booked. You don't want a tricky patient situation on top of an inspection.

5. Block emergency and cleaning time into the diary, so zoning and emergency readiness visibly happen and aren't skipped.

6. Make sure everyone knows where the emergency kit is today, especially if it's recently moved. Oxygen, defib and drugs: every person, no hesitation.

7. Everyone reads their own questions beforehand. Each person reviews what an inspector is likely to ask their role, and can answer in their own words. Confident, not reciting.

8. Hold a calm morning huddle. Reset nerves, confirm roles, remind everyone of the kit location and the light-diary plan.

✅ Action steps

2. Ask three team members where the emergency kit, oxygen and defib are. Did they all answer straight away?

75598002.title: 4. What inspectors ask your team (with model answers)
75598002.html:
⏱ 15 minutes · 🎯 A practice question sheet covering the 10 questions inspectors ask receptionists and dental nurses, with each team member's gaps marked after a 10-minute run-through.

The Specialist Dental Advisor will talk to your team directly. Here are real questions they ask, with strong answers to prepare from. Teach the idea, not a script, and let people say it in their own words.

💬 Receptionists

• "Do you understand Duty of Candour?" When something goes wrong, we apologise to the person and offer support or a remedy to put it right where we can.

• "Do you know where the emergency kit is?" Name the exact place, and know it's signposted.

• "How do you report a safeguarding concern?" Use the contact details and flowchart in the practice, call 999 if someone is in immediate danger, and know social services can be contacted.

• "Is patient information kept out of view when reception is empty?" Yes: nothing left on the desk, screens locked, papers shredded. Expect "show me your desk right now".

• "How do you handle patients in pain?" We hold emergency slots and never turn a patient in pain away.

💬 Dental nurses

• "Walk me through decontamination." Closed, lidded transport box, never hand-handle sharp instruments, follow the decon room poster for PPE, the same process every day. Expect "show me".

• "How do you validate the autoclave?" Daily checks confirm it reaches 134°C and holds for 2 minutes, logged every day, serviced every year. Expect "show me today's log".

• "How do you prevent wrong-site treatment?" Confirm name and date of birth, show the patient which tooth, check the treatment plan, and get verbal and written consent.

• "Who is your Radiation Protection Supervisor?" A name. Make sure everyone knows it.

• "What would you do right now after a needlestick from a high-risk patient?" Know your sharps injury flowchart, including assessing the source patient's risk.

✅ Action steps

1. Run a 10-minute "inspector questions" round at your next team meeting.

2. Make sure everyone can name your Radiation Protection Supervisor, safeguarding lead and first aider.

3. Post in the discussion: which question tripped your team up?

75598002.title: 5. Close the loop: audits, evidence and gaps
75598002.html:
⏱ 15 minutes · 🎯 Your last infection control audit checked for an action plan and re-audit date, plus a working actions log showing finding, owner, deadline and done date.

Inspectors want to see what you did about what you found. That's the difference between "we have an audit" and good governance.

🔁 The evidence chain: requirement → policy → training → staff know it → record → audit → finding → action → re-audit. Not everything needs the full chain (a displayed certificate is just there), but anything clinical or safeguarding usually does.

📉 A low audit score is fine, if the loop is closed. A poor infection control or radiograph audit is acceptable when it has an action plan attached and a documented re-audit 3–6 months later showing improvement. An audit with no action is weak evidence. Keep the last two infection control and radiograph audits on file, not just the latest.

🛠️ If an inspector finds a gap, follow the pattern that works in real inspections: acknowledge it → fix it promptly → document the fix with a date → be ready to show it. Real examples include a CCTV impact assessment signed two days after a visit, a lone-worker risk assessment updated with a new control within days, and X-ray testing booked with named dates. Evidence created soon after a finding, clearly in response to it, can still be considered. So can evidence you already had but didn't produce on the day.

🙋 Be open. Owning a gap, logging it and explaining the fix goes down far better than being defensive.

✅ Action steps

1. Pull your last infection control audit. Does it have an action plan, and a re-audit booked?

2. Start a simple "actions log": finding, owner, deadline, done date.

3. Post in the discussion: what's one audit action you've closed recently? Celebrate it.
